set1.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of blood disorders
set1.q: In acute leukemia, acquired mutations in which genes block the differentiation of immature cells?
opts: Rearranging immunoglobulin genes is NORMAL B-cell development (V(D)J recombination in the marrow). Maturation arrest comes from acquired mutations in transcription factors.
Coagulation-factor genes are not tied to leukemic maturation arrest. In acute leukemia, the block in differentiation comes from acquired mutations in transcription factors.
Red-cell membrane genes are not tied to leukemic maturation arrest. The block in differentiation of immature lymphoid or myeloid cells comes from acquired mutations in transcription factors.
Correct. Acquired mutations in transcription factors, which regulate the differentiation of immature lymphoid or myeloid cells, produce the maturation arrest of acute leukemia.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 20

set1.io: Review the functions of blood cells
set1.q: Into which cells do activated, selected B cells differentiate?
opts: T cells or natural killer cells
T cells and natural killer cells are separate lymphoid lines from the lymphoid progenitor, not products of B-cell activation. Selected B cells become plasma cells or memory B cells.
Plasma cells or memory B cells
Correct. After antigen activation and selection, B cells differentiate into plasma cells (which produce antibody) or memory B cells.
Lymphoblasts and myeloblasts are the immature malignant cells of acute leukemia. Normal activated, selected B cells differentiate into plasma cells or memory B cells.
Monocytes and their macrophages are myeloid cells. Activated, selected B cells differentiate into plasma cells or memory B cells.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 15, 24

set1.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set1.q: What does von Willebrand factor do?
opts: Activates factor X together with factor IXa
Activating factor X is the job of IXa with its cofactor VIIIa. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and carries and stabilizes factor VIII.
Degrades fibrin once a clot has formed
Degrading fibrin is plasmin's job in fibrinolysis. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and carries and stabilizes factor VIII.
Supports platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII
Correct. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and carries and stabilizes factor VIII, which is why von Willebrand disease is listed with the hemophilias as a bleeding disorder.
Limits coagulation together with protein S
Activated protein C with protein S (and antithrombin) limits coagulation. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
set1.q: Which consequences do monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration cause in myeloma?
opts: Leukostasis in the lungs and brain

Leukostasis is impaired microcirculation from a high white-cell burden, often in the lungs or brain. Myeloma's monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity.
Thrombosis with a falling platelet count
Thrombosis despite a falling platelet count is immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Myeloma's proteins and marrow infiltration cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity.
Renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity
Correct. In multiple myeloma, monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration can cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity; altered bone remodeling adds osteolytic lesions and hypercalcemia.
A hematocrit raised by reduced plasma volume is relative erythrocytosis. Myeloma's marrow infiltration causes anemia, along with renal injury and impaired immunity.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 27

set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: Microcytic hypochromic anemias are caused by disorders of what?
opts: Correct. Microcytic hypochromic anemias are caused by disorders of hemoglobin synthesis, which is why iron deficiency, thalassemia and sideroblastic anemia sit in the microcytic group.
Impaired maturation of erythroid precursors in the marrow is the usual story of the MACROCYTIC anemias. Small, pale cells point to a disorder of hemoglobin synthesis.
A membrane defect makes rigid spherocytes that the spleen destroys: hemolysis, not microcytic hypochromia. Small pale cells come from disordered hemoglobin synthesis.
Shortened survival is hemolysis, a destruction mechanism. Microcytic hypochromic anemias are a production problem: disorders of hemoglobin synthesis.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 32, 33

set1.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set1.q: What does the PT (prothrombin time) assess?
opts: Intrinsic factors XII, XI, IX and VIII
The intrinsic factors are assessed by the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time), not the PT. The PT assesses extrinsic factor VII and the common factors.
Extrinsic factor VII and the common factors

Correct. The PT (prothrombin time) assesses the extrinsic factor (VII) and the common factors (X, V, II and I); the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) assesses the intrinsic factors XII, XI, IX and VIII plus the common ones.
Plasminogen becoming plasmin to degrade fibrin is fibrinolysis, a separate process. The PT assesses extrinsic factor VII and the common factors.
Platelet adhesion via von Willebrand factor
Platelet adhesion is a platelet function that von Willebrand factor supports. The PT assesses the coagulation factors: extrinsic VII and the common factors.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
set1.q: Which appearance identifies a band neutrophil on a smear?
opts: Two-lobed nucleus with large red secondary granules
A nucleus with two lobes and red secondary granules is the eosinophil. The band neutrophil has a single kidney-bean nucleus indented more than half its width.
Round nucleus with scant pale cytoplasm, no granules
A round mature nucleus with clumped chromatin and scant light blue cytoplasm without granules is the lymphocyte. The band has a kidney-bean nucleus indented more than half its width.
Two to three lobes hidden by dark granules
A mature nucleus of two to three lobes obscured by numerous basophilic granules is the basophil. The band neutrophil has one kidney-bean nucleus indented more than half its width.
Kidney-bean nucleus indented over half its width
Correct. A band neutrophil has a kidney-bean nucleus with mature chromatin and no nucleoli, an indentation greater than half the diameter, and secondary granules only.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 13, 14

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set1.q: Why must both the relative and the absolute white cell counts be read?
opts: A fall in one type can falsely raise another's percentage

Correct. Percentages are shares of one total, so an absolute decrease in one cell type can show an artificially increased relative count in another. Reading the absolute count shows whether that cell really rose.
The relative count gives the number of cells per microliter
That describes the absolute count. The relative count is a percentage of the white cells; the absolute count, total white count times that fraction, is the number per microliter.
Each cell's percentage is measured apart from the others
The percentages are not independent: they are shares of one total, so when one cell type falls in absolute terms another's percentage can rise artificially. That is why both counts must be read.
The absolute count ignores the total white blood cell count
The absolute count is built from the total: white blood cell count times the cell's fraction. It is the relative percentage alone that can mislead when another cell type falls.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set1.q: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a malignancy of which cells?
opts: A neoplasm of mature B cells is chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a malignancy of PRECURSOR B or T cells.
Germinal-center B cells give rise to classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia arises from precursor B or T cells.
Differentiated antibody-producing B-lineage cells give plasma-cell myeloma. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia arises from precursor B or T cells.

Correct. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is a malignancy of precursor B or T cells (lymphoblasts): B-ALL/LBL from the B-cell precursor in the marrow, T-ALL/LBL from the T-cell precursor in the thymus.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 23, 28

set1.topic: Anemia by cell size and marrow response
set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: Which anemia is listed in the microcytic group?
opts: Megaloblastic anemia, from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, is MACROCYTIC (above 100 fL). Sideroblastic anemia is the microcytic one here.
Correct. The microcytic group (mean cell volume below 80 fL, femtoliters) lists iron deficiency, thalassemia, inflammation in some cases, and sideroblastic anemia.
Marrow failure or infiltration is listed under the NORMOCYTIC anemias (80 to 100 fL). Sideroblastic anemia is the microcytic one here.
Inflammation or renal disease is listed under the normocytic anemias. Sideroblastic anemia belongs to the microcytic group with iron deficiency and thalassemia.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
set1.q: What is the primary pathogenic defect in acute leukemia?
opts: Correct. The primary pathogenic defect in acute leukemia is maturation arrest: acquired mutations in transcription factors block differentiation, and other mutations let the cells proliferate independently of growth factors.
Ineffective hematopoiesis with dysplasia defines the myelodysplastic neoplasms, which can progress to acute myeloid leukemia. The primary defect in acute leukemia is maturation arrest.
Shortened red-cell survival is hemolysis, a red-cell disorder. The primary pathogenic defect in acute leukemia is maturation arrest of immature lymphoid or myeloid cells.
A reactive rise is a normal marrow answering a signal, not a malignant defect. Acute leukemia's primary pathogenic defect is maturation arrest from acquired mutations.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 20

set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: What is relative erythrocytosis?
opts: An increased red-cell mass is ABSOLUTE erythrocytosis. Relative erythrocytosis has no extra red cells: the plasma volume is reduced.
A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm raising red-cell mass is polycythemia vera, an absolute erythrocytosis. Relative erythrocytosis is reduced plasma volume.
Less plasma without more red-cell mass
Correct. Relative erythrocytosis is reduced plasma volume without increased red-cell mass, such as dehydration; hemoglobin and hematocrit rise only because the plasma has shrunk.
An erythropoietic response to hypoxia or increased erythropoietin is secondary erythrocytosis, which raises red-cell mass. Relative erythrocytosis is reduced plasma volume.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 41

set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: Under the World Health Organization 2024 cutoffs (ages 15 to 65), below what hemoglobin is a nonpregnant woman anemic?
opts: Too low. The World Health Organization 2024 cutoff for nonpregnant women aged 15 to 65 is a hemoglobin below 12 g/dL.
Too low. The World Health Organization 2024 cutoff for nonpregnant women aged 15 to 65 is below 12 g/dL.
Correct. The World Health Organization 2024 cutoffs for ages 15 to 65 are a hemoglobin below 13 g/dL in men and below 12 g/dL in nonpregnant women.
Below 13 g/dL is the World Health Organization 2024 cutoff for MEN aged 15 to 65. For nonpregnant women it is below 12 g/dL.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set1.q: Which three causes should a raised eosinophil count bring to mind first?
opts: Chronic infections such as cytomegalovirus and tuberculosis are listed for a raised MONOCYTE count. For eosinophils the three first thoughts are allergy, parasites and drug effects.
Correct. Think of three things with increased eosinophils: allergy (especially asthma), a parasite, or a drug effect. Eosinophilia can rarely be neoplastic or autoimmune.
Acute bacterial inflammation goes with neutrophilia, and a band rise with infection. A raised eosinophil count points first to allergy, parasites or a drug effect.
Eosinophilia can be neoplastic, but only rarely; malignancy is a consideration if BASOPHILS are elevated. For eosinophils, think first of allergy, parasites and drug effects.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 12, 13

set1.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
set1.q: In the healthy adult, where does almost all hematopoiesis occur?
opts: Distal radius, tibia and the small hand bones

Wrong end of the limbs. Adult hematopoiesis occurs almost entirely in the axial skeleton and the PROXIMAL humerus and femur; the distal long bones and hand bones are not named as sites of adult blood production.
The thymus and the peripheral lymph nodes

The thymus is where T-cell precursors develop after leaving the marrow, not where blood cells are produced. Adult hematopoiesis takes place in the marrow of the axial skeleton and proximal humerus and femur.
The spleen and the liver sinusoids
Neither the spleen nor the liver is given as a site of adult blood production. Most hematopoiesis occurs in the bone marrow, almost all of it in the axial skeleton and proximal humerus and femur.
Axial skeleton, proximal humerus and femur
Correct. Most hematopoiesis occurs in the bone marrow, and in the healthy adult almost all of it is in the axial skeleton plus the proximal humerus and femur.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 4

set1.topic: Anemia by cell size and marrow response
set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: Which deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia?
opts: Correct. In the macrocytic group (mean cell volume above 100 fL, femtoliters), the megaloblastic causes are vitamin B12 or folate deficiency; liver disease, alcohol, drugs and reticulocytosis are the nonmegaloblastic causes.
Iron deficiency is a disorder of hemoglobin synthesis and sits in the MICROCYTIC group (early on, normocytic). The megaloblastic causes are vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
Liver disease and alcohol do cause macrocytosis, but they are listed as NONmegaloblastic causes. Megaloblastic anemia comes from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
Thalassemia is a microcytic anemia, a disorder of hemoglobin synthesis. Megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia comes from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set1.q: What does plasmin do?
opts: Factor X is activated by tissue factor-VIIa at initiation and by IXa with VIIIa. Plasmin degrades fibrin.
Correct. In fibrinolysis, plasminogen becomes plasmin, which degrades fibrin; this is separate from the regulation of coagulation by antithrombin and activated protein C.
Crosslinking fibrin is the work of factor XIIIa, which stabilizes the clot. Plasmin does the opposite: it degrades fibrin.
Thrombin (IIa) converts fibrinogen (I) to fibrin. Plasmin, formed from plasminogen, degrades fibrin.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set1.q: How is an absolute neutrophil count of 750 cells/µL graded?
opts: Agranulocytosis needs a count below 200 cells/µL. At 750 the count sits in the moderate band, 500 to 1,000 cells/µL.
Severe neutropenia is below 500 cells/µL. A count of 750 is above that line, in the moderate band of 500 to 1,000.
Correct. An absolute neutrophil count of 750 cells/µL falls in the moderate band, 500 to 1,000 cells/µL; severe is below 500 and mild is 1,000 to 1,500.
Mild neutropenia is 1,000 to 1,500 cells/µL. A count of 750 is below that band, in moderate neutropenia (500 to 1,000).
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of blood disorders
set1.q: In V(D)J recombination, which gene segments do light chains use?
opts: Correct. Developing B cells rearrange their immunoglobulin genes in the marrow: heavy chains use V, D and J segments, while light chains use only V and J.
All three segments are used by HEAVY chains. Light chains have no D segment in their rearrangement; they use V and J only.
Light chains do not use a D segment at all; D belongs only to the heavy-chain rearrangement (V, D and J). Light chains join V to J.
D and J both appear in the heavy-chain rearrangement, but light chains lack D. Light chains rearrange V with J.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set1.q: What is bandemia?
opts: More mature neutrophils in the blood
A rise in mature neutrophils is neutrophilia. Bandemia specifically means more IMMATURE neutrophils, the band forms, in the circulation: a left shift.
That is agranulocytosis, profound neutropenia. Bandemia is an increase, not a loss: more immature band neutrophils in the blood.
More eosinophils from a drug effect
A drug effect is one of the three things to think of with eosinophilia. Bandemia concerns neutrophils: an increase in their immature band forms.
More immature neutrophils in the blood
Correct. Bandemia is an increase in immature (band) neutrophils, a left shift, which may accompany infection or other inflammatory stress.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 10

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set1.q: Which two features classify the lymphoid neoplasms?
opts: The peripheral count can be low, normal or high in the same disease, so it cannot classify. Lymphoid neoplasms are classified by lineage and stage of maturation.
Clonality alone does not establish malignancy, and the count varies. Classification uses the cell's lineage and its stage of maturation.
Neither age nor cell size is the classifier. Lymphoid neoplasms are classified by cell lineage (B, T or natural killer) and stage of maturation (precursor or mature).
Cell lineage and stage of maturation

Correct. Lymphoid neoplasms are classified by cell lineage and stage of maturation: precursor B or T cells, mature B cells, mature T and natural killer cells, and germinal-center B cells for classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 23

set1.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set1.q: After initiation, which enzyme-cofactor pair activates factor X?
opts: Xa with its cofactor Va acts one step later: it converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa). Factor X is activated by IXa with VIIIa.
Thrombin and XIIIa act at the end: thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin and XIIIa crosslinks it. Factor X is activated by IXa with VIIIa.
Correct. In the factor X activation step, IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activates X to Xa; Xa with Va then generates thrombin.
Plasmin degrades fibrin in fibrinolysis, and protein S helps activated protein C limit coagulation. Factor X is activated by IXa with VIIIa.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

set1.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myeloproliferative syndromes
set1.q: Which disorder is one of the myeloproliferative neoplasms?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenia is not among the myeloproliferative neoplasms, which are chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Watch the ending: thrombocythemia, not thrombocytopenia.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a mature B-cell neoplasm, a lymphoid disease. The myeloproliferative neoplasms are myeloid: chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis.

Hereditary spherocytosis is not among the myeloproliferative neoplasms (chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis). Essential thrombocythemia is the one listed here.
Correct. The myeloproliferative neoplasms are chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis: clonal proliferations of myeloid cells.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of blood disorders
set1.q: What is the cause of factor V Leiden thrombophilia?
opts: Correct. Factor V Leiden is a thrombophilia (excessive clotting) caused by a genetic mutation; antiphospholipid syndrome, the other thrombophilia listed, is an autoimmune response.
An autoimmune response causes antiphospholipid syndrome, the other thrombophilia. Factor V Leiden is a genetic mutation.
Factor V Leiden causes excessive clotting, not the bleeding a deficiency would; the bleeding deficiencies listed are factor VIII and IX (hemophilia A and B). Its cause is a genetic mutation.
An immune reaction to heparin is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a platelet disorder. Factor V Leiden is a genetic mutation.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: In hereditary spherocytosis, why are the red cells destroyed early?
opts: Antibodies lyse the cells within the circulation
The sequence shows no antibody and no lysis in the blood: spherocytes are trapped in the spleen and destroyed by splenic macrophages.
Their hemoglobin synthesis fails in the marrow
Failed hemoglobin synthesis makes small, pale (microcytic hypochromic) cells, a production problem. Spherocytes are destroyed because they are rigid and get trapped in the spleen.
Rigid spherocytes are trapped and eaten in the spleen

Correct. Biconcave young cells lose lipid membrane on repeated passage through the spleen and circulation, become rigid, inflexible spherocytes, are trapped in the spleen and destroyed prematurely by splenic macrophages: extravascular hemolysis.
The marrow releases them before they mature
Early release of immature cells describes a left shift of neutrophils, not spherocytosis. Spherocytes are released as normal biconcave cells and become rigid as they lose membrane.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: What is the usual red-cell lifespan that hemolysis shortens?
opts: Far too short for a normal red cell. Red-cell survival is usually about 120 days; hemolytic anemia shortens it below that.
Too short. The usual red-cell lifespan is about 120 days, and hemolysis is defined by survival shortened below it.

Correct. In hemolytic anemia red-cell survival is shortened below the usual lifespan of about 120 days, hemoglobin breakdown products increase, and a compensating marrow raises reticulocyte production.
Too long. The usual red-cell lifespan is about 120 days; hemolysis shortens survival below that.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 37

set1.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myeloproliferative syndromes
set1.q: Which process defines the myeloproliferative neoplasms?
opts: Correct. Myeloproliferative neoplasms are a clonal proliferation of myeloid cells: chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis.
Ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia defines the myelodysplastic neoplasms. The myeloproliferative neoplasms are a clonal proliferation of myeloid cells.
Impaired differentiation with abnormal blast proliferation is acute myeloid leukemia. The myeloproliferative neoplasms are a clonal proliferation of myeloid cells.
Clonal growth of antibody-making B cells
A clonal malignancy of differentiated antibody-producing B-lineage cells is plasma-cell myeloma, a lymphoid neoplasm. The myeloproliferative neoplasms are clonal proliferations of MYELOID cells.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: What does hypochromia of red cells reflect?
opts: Reduced size is microcytosis, described by the size terms (normocytic, microcytic, macrocytic). Hypochromia is about color, the degree of hemoglobinization.

Correct. The degree of hemoglobinization is reflected in the color of red cells: normochromic or hypochromic. Hypochromic cells carry less hemoglobin, as in the microcytic hypochromic anemias of impaired hemoglobin synthesis.
Shape is the third morphologic clue, separate from color. Hypochromia describes reduced hemoglobinization seen as paler red cells.
Increased volume is macrocytosis, a size term. Hypochromia is a color term: reduced hemoglobinization of the red cell.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 31, 32

set1.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set1.q: Which anemia results from diminished erythropoiesis?
opts: Correct. The anemias of diminished erythropoiesis are megaloblastic anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency anemia, iron deficiency anemia and aplastic anemia: too little production rather than loss or destruction.
Hereditary spherocytosis is a hemolytic anemia: rigid spherocytes are destroyed in the spleen. Aplastic anemia is the anemia of diminished erythropoiesis here.
Blood-loss anemia is loss of formed cells, and the marrow answers with an increased reticulocyte response. Aplastic anemia is a failure of production.
Extravascular hemolysis is premature destruction within phagocytes. Aplastic anemia is the anemia of diminished erythropoiesis.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
set1.q: Which progenitor gives rise to megakaryocytes?
opts: The lymphoid progenitor gives B cells, T cells and natural killer cells, none of which make platelets. Megakaryocytes sit on the myeloid branch with erythroid precursors, granulocytes and monocytes.

Correct. In the simplified lineage model the multipotent stem cell gives myeloid and lymphoid progenitors, and the myeloid progenitor gives erythroid precursors, megakaryocytes (which make platelets), granulocytes and monocytes.
The erythroid precursor is a sister product of the myeloid progenitor, and it matures into erythrocytes. Megakaryocytes come from the myeloid progenitor directly and make platelets.
The granulocyte line gives neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils. Megakaryocytes are a separate product of the myeloid progenitor, and they make platelets rather than granulocytes.
set1.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set2.q: What is extravascular hemolysis?
opts: Correct. In the majority of hemolytic anemias the premature destruction of red cells occurs within phagocytes, the same cells that normally remove old red cells; this is called extravascular hemolysis.
Destruction within the circulation is the other route, intravascular hemolysis. Extravascular hemolysis is premature destruction inside phagocytes.
Losing red cells from the vessels is blood-loss anemia, not hemolysis. Extravascular hemolysis is premature destruction of red cells within phagocytes.
Failure of red-cell production in marrow
Failed production is anemia of diminished erythropoiesis, such as aplastic anemia. Extravascular hemolysis is a destruction mechanism: premature removal within phagocytes.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 38, 39

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set2.q: Which factors make up the common pathway?
opts: XII, XI, IX and VIII are the INTRINSIC factors the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) assesses. The common pathway is X, V, II and I.
Tissue factor with VII is the extrinsic start, assessed by the PT (prothrombin time). The common pathway is X, V, II and I.
VIII and IX are intrinsic factors, and XIII crosslinks fibrin. The common pathway is X, V, II and I.
Correct. The common pathway is factors X, V, II and I, which generate thrombin and fibrin; both the PT (prothrombin time) and the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) assess it.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

set2.topic: Anemia by cell size and marrow response
set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set2.q: Early iron deficiency usually falls in which mean cell volume group?
opts: Correct. Established iron deficiency is microcytic, but EARLY iron deficiency is listed with the normocytic anemias (mean cell volume 80 to 100 fL, femtoliters), before the cells have shrunk.
Iron deficiency becomes microcytic once established, but the early stage is listed in the normocytic group (80 to 100 fL, femtoliters).
Macrocytic anemias come from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency or from liver disease, alcohol, drugs or reticulocytosis. Early iron deficiency is normocytic.
Megaloblastic anemia is the vitamin B12 or folate subset of the macrocytic group. Early iron deficiency is normocytic, later microcytic.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myelodysplastic syndromes
set2.q: Which bone marrow neoplasm is defined by ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia?
opts: Correct. Myelodysplastic neoplasms (the World Health Organization's term; myelodysplastic syndromes remains in use elsewhere) show ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia, and they can progress to acute myeloid leukemia.

Myeloproliferative neoplasms are clonal PROLIFERATION of myeloid cells: chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Ineffective hematopoiesis with dysplasia defines the myelodysplastic neoplasms.

Acute myeloid leukemia is a myeloid malignancy with impaired differentiation and abnormal blast proliferation, distinct from the dysplastic process. Ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia is the myelodysplastic neoplasm.
Myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell malignancy of the B lineage, not a myeloid neoplasm. Ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia defines the myelodysplastic neoplasms.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 18

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myeloproliferative syndromes
set2.q: On the myeloid branch, which neoplasm arises from the red-cell line?
opts: Essential thrombocythemia (and megakaryocytic leukemia) arises from the megakaryocyte line. Polycythemia vera arises from the red-cell line.
Correct. In the division of hematologic neoplasms by lineage, the red-cell line of the myeloid stem cell gives polycythemia vera and erythroid leukemia.
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is on the lymphoid branch, a mature B-cell neoplasm. On the myeloid branch, the red-cell line gives polycythemia vera.
Monocytic leukemia arises from the monocyte line of the myeloid branch. The red-cell line gives polycythemia vera and erythroid leukemia.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of platelet disorders
set2.q: What happens in immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
opts: Bleeding from the falling platelet count
A falling count would be expected to bleed, but in immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia platelet activation causes thrombosis despite the falling count.
Reduced marrow production is a separate cause of thrombocytopenia. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an immune drug reaction in which platelet activation causes thrombosis.
A clonal rise in the platelet count
A clonal marrow disorder causes PRIMARY thrombocytosis, a rising count. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia lowers the count while activated platelets cause thrombosis.
Thrombosis despite a falling platelet count
Correct. In immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, platelet activation causes thrombosis despite a falling count, so a low count does not mean a bleeding tendency here.

set2.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
set2.q: Where do T-cell precursors develop?
opts: The bone marrow is where the B-cell precursor develops. T-cell precursors develop in the thymus.
Correct. The lymphoid progenitor branches into the B-cell precursor in the bone marrow and the T-cell precursor in the thymus, the origin of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.
Germinal centers are where activated B cells undergo somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation. T-cell precursors develop in the thymus.
The spleen is not where T-cell precursors develop. The lymphoid progenitor branches into the B-cell precursor in the bone marrow and the T-cell precursor in the thymus.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 24

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set2.q: Which absolute neutrophil count defines severe neutropenia?
opts: That cut-off is agranulocytosis, deeper than severe neutropenia. Severe neutropenia is an absolute neutrophil count below 500 cells/µL.

Correct. Neutropenia is graded by absolute neutrophil count: mild 1,000 to 1,500, moderate 500 to 1,000, severe below 500 cells/µL, and agranulocytosis below 200. Severe neutropenia increases the risk of serious infection.
This range is moderate neutropenia. Severe neutropenia begins below 500 cells/µL.
This range is mild neutropenia. Severe neutropenia is an absolute neutrophil count below 500 cells/µL.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set2.q: How is a relative white cell count converted to an absolute count?
opts: Multiply the total white count by the cell's fraction
Correct. The absolute count is the white blood cell count times the relative count expressed as a fraction: a total of 8,000 cells/µL with 25 percent neutrophils gives 2,000 neutrophils/µL.
Divide the cell's percentage by the total white count
Dividing gives a meaningless small number. The conversion multiplies: total white blood cell count times the relative count as a fraction gives cells per microliter.
Subtract the lymphocyte count from the total white count
Subtraction would lump every non-lymphocyte together. Each cell's absolute count is found by multiplying the total white blood cell count by that cell's relative fraction.
Read the cell's percentage straight off the differential
The percentage is the relative count itself, not the absolute one. To get cells per microliter, multiply the total white blood cell count by that percentage as a fraction.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set2.q: Which three morphologic features give etiologic clues in anemia?
opts: Nuclear lobes describe white cells (eosinophils, basophils, neutrophils); mature red cells are judged by size, hemoglobinization (color) and shape.

Correct. The morphologic characteristics that provide etiologic clues are red-cell size (normocytic, microcytic or macrocytic), degree of hemoglobinization seen as color (normochromic or hypochromic), and shape.
A count says how many cells there are, not what they look like, and granules are not among the listed red-cell clues. The morphologic clues are size, hemoglobinization (color) and shape.
Lifespan and where cells are removed concern hemolysis, not what the smear shows. The morphologic clues are size, hemoglobinization (color) and shape.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
set2.q: Which leukocyte normally makes up the largest share of the total white cell count?
opts: Lymphocytes are the second-largest group, at 20 to 40 percent of the total leukocyte count. Neutrophils, at 40 to 60 percent, make up the largest share.
Monocytes are a small group, 2 to 8 percent of the total leukocyte count. Neutrophils, at 40 to 60 percent, make up the largest share.
Correct. Neutrophils are normally 40 to 60 percent of the total leukocyte count, the largest share, ahead of lymphocytes at 20 to 40 percent.
Eosinophils are only 1 to 4 percent of the total leukocyte count. Neutrophils, at 40 to 60 percent, make up the largest share; basophils are the smallest at 0.5 to 1 percent.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 6

set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set2.q: What is anemia primarily defined by?
opts: Hematocrit, the share of blood volume occupied by red cells, provides supporting information only. Anemia is defined primarily by hemoglobin below the cutoff for age, sex and pregnancy status.
A red-cell count below the reference range
The red-cell count appears among the reference intervals, but it is not the defining measure. Anemia is defined primarily by hemoglobin below the cutoff for age, sex and pregnancy status.
Hemoglobin below the cutoff for the person
Correct. Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, and it is defined primarily by hemoglobin below the cutoff for age, sex and pregnancy status; hematocrit only supports.
A mean cell volume outside 80 to 100 fL
Mean cell volume classifies an anemia that already exists (microcytic, normocytic, macrocytic); it does not define anemia. Hemoglobin below the cutoff does.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set2.q: Which pair converts prothrombin to thrombin?
opts: IXa with VIIIa is the step BEFORE: it activates factor X. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by Xa with Va.
Correct. In thrombin generation, Xa with its cofactor Va converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa); thrombin then turns fibrinogen (I) into fibrin.
Tissue factor-VIIa starts the sequence by activating IX and X. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by Xa with Va.
XIIIa acts on fibrin at the very end, producing crosslinked fibrin. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by Xa with Va.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

set2.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
set2.q: How does multiple myeloma produce hypercalcemia?
opts: Correct. In myeloma, altered bone remodeling can produce osteolytic lesions and hypercalcemia; the monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration separately cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity.
Monoclonal proteins injure the kidneys, but that is the renal consequence. Hypercalcemia comes from altered bone remodeling, the same process that makes osteolytic lesions.
Marrow infiltration explains the anemia of myeloma. Hypercalcemia comes from altered bone remodeling with osteolytic lesions.
Impaired immunity is another consequence of the monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration. Hypercalcemia arises from altered bone remodeling.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 27

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set2.q: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplasm of which cells?
opts: Precursor B cells (lymphoblasts) give B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplasm of MATURE B cells.
Mature T and natural killer cells give their own distinct neoplasms. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplasm of mature B cells.
Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a mature B-cell neoplasm, related to small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL).
A malignancy of differentiated plasma cells is myeloma. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia arises from mature B cells and is related to small lymphocytic lymphoma.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 23, 28

set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set2.q: Macrocytic anemias often stem from abnormalities that impair what?
opts: Disorders of hemoglobin synthesis give the MICROCYTIC hypochromic anemias. Large cells point instead to impaired maturation of erythroid precursors in the marrow.
Shortened survival defines hemolytic anemia, a destruction mechanism. Macrocytic anemias usually reflect impaired maturation of erythroid precursors in the marrow.
Plasma volume changes shift concentrations (as in relative erythrocytosis) without changing cell size. Macrocytosis reflects impaired maturation of erythroid precursors.
Correct. Macrocytic anemias often stem from abnormalities that impair the maturation of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, as in the megaloblastic anemias of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 32, 33

set2.io: Review the functions of blood cells
set2.q: Which leukocyte binds IgE (immunoglobulin E)?
opts: Correct. Basophils bind IgE (immunoglobulin E) and take part in the parasite response and allergy; few should be seen on a normal complete blood count, so a rise should prompt thought of malignancy.
Neutrophils are phagocytic first responders to infection, not the IgE-binding cell. The leukocyte that binds IgE (immunoglobulin E) is the basophil.
Monocytes are precursors to macrophages, raised in chronic infection or chronic myelomonocytic leukemia. The IgE (immunoglobulin E)-binding leukocyte is the basophil.
Natural killer cells are lymphocytes from the lymphoid progenitor. The leukocyte that binds IgE (immunoglobulin E) in allergy and the parasite response is the basophil.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 13

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myeloproliferative syndromes
set2.q: What kind of disorder is polycythemia vera?
opts: A marrow response to hypoxia or raised erythropoietin is SECONDARY erythrocytosis, a reaction to a stimulus. Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm.
A fall in plasma from dehydration
Reduced plasma volume with normal red-cell mass is relative erythrocytosis. Polycythemia vera is an absolute increase from a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm.
Myelodysplastic neoplasms show ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias, the opposite of an excess. Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm.

Correct. Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm: an absolute erythrocytosis from clonal proliferation of myeloid cells, listed with chronic myeloid leukemia, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 41, 18

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set2.q: What initiates physiologic coagulation?
opts: Factor XII belongs to the intrinsic factors the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) assesses in the laboratory. Physiologic initiation is tissue factor-VIIa activating IX and X.
Correct. Physiologic initiation is tissue factor-VIIa activating factors IX and X; external bleeding is not required.
External bleeding is not required. Physiologic coagulation is initiated when tissue factor-VIIa activates factors IX and X.
Thrombin acting on fibrinogen is the fibrin-formation step at the END of the reactions. Initiation is tissue factor-VIIa activating IX and X.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
set2.q: How does the Sepsis-3 definition describe sepsis?
opts: Immature bands above 10 percent of white cells
A band count above 10 percent was a HISTORICAL criterion of systemic inflammatory response syndrome. Sepsis-3 defines sepsis by infection-associated, life-threatening organ dysfunction.
Neutrophilia often accompanies acute bacterial inflammation, but a raised count is not the definition. Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as infection-associated, life-threatening organ dysfunction.
Severe neutropenia increases the risk of serious infection, but it does not define sepsis. Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as infection-associated, life-threatening organ dysfunction.

Correct. Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as infection-associated, life-threatening organ dysfunction; the band count above 10 percent was a historical criterion of the older systemic inflammatory response syndrome definition.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 10

set2.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
set2.q: In leukemia, what can the peripheral white blood cell count be?
opts: Correct. The peripheral white blood cell count in leukemia may be low, normal or high, because marrow involvement can suppress normal blood-cell production while malignant cells may or may not spill into the blood.
High, because blasts spill into the blood
Some leukemias do show a high count, even hyperleukocytosis, but a high count is not required. Marrow involvement can suppress normal production, so the count may be low, normal or high.
Low, because blasts stay in the marrow
Marrow suppression can lower the count, but it is not the only pattern: the peripheral count in leukemia may be low, normal or high.
Leukostasis is impaired microcirculation with organ injury, and a high count alone does not establish it. The peripheral count in leukemia may be low, normal or high from the start.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 21, 22

set2.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
set2.q: Approximately what share of whole blood is plasma?
opts: Too low. Whole blood is about 55 percent plasma and 45 percent formed elements, so 35 percent understates the fluid fraction by roughly 20 points.

This is the share of the formed elements (red cells, white cells and platelets), not of plasma. Whole blood is about 55 percent plasma and 45 percent formed elements; the two figures are easy to swap.
Correct. Whole blood is approximately 55 percent plasma and 45 percent formed elements, and plasma itself is about 90 to 92 percent water carrying electrolytes, nutrients, wastes and proteins.
Too high. Plasma is about 55 percent of whole blood, with the formed elements making up the remaining 45 percent. A 65 percent plasma share would leave the cells at only about a third.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 3

set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set2.q: What does anemia reduce?
opts: Anemia is a fall in hemoglobin, not in plasma; a reduced plasma volume with normal red-cell mass is relative erythrocytosis. Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity.
Clotting factors belong to the plasma and the coagulation reactions. Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
Correct. Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, which is why it is defined by hemoglobin below the cutoff for age, sex and pregnancy status.
Suppressed white-cell production is part of leukemic cytopenias, not the meaning of anemia. Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

set2.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
set2.q: Hemophilia A is a deficiency of which factor?
opts: Factor IX deficiency is hemophilia B. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
Factor V is the factor altered in factor V Leiden, a genetic thrombophilia, not a bleeding deficiency. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
Correct. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency; hemophilia B is factor IX deficiency. Both factors work together, IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activating factor X.
Factor VII is the extrinsic factor the PT (prothrombin time) assesses. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

set2.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
set2.q: Which organs does leukostasis often involve?
opts: Correct. Leukostasis is impaired microcirculation with organ injury, often involving the lungs or the brain.
The liver and spleen are not the organs named for leukostasis. Its impaired microcirculation with organ injury often involves the lungs or the brain.
Kidney injury and osteolytic bone lesions are consequences of multiple myeloma. Leukostasis often involves the lungs or the brain.
The marrow and thymus are where blood cells and T-cell precursors develop. The microcirculatory organ injury of leukostasis often involves the lungs or the brain.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
set2.q: Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of which cells?
opts: Precursor B cells (lymphoblasts) give B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Myeloma arises far later in the B pathway, from differentiated plasma cells.
Mature B cells give chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma. Myeloma is a malignancy of the differentiated end of the line, the plasma cell.
Despite the similar name, myeloma is not a myeloid neoplasm. It is a clonal plasma-cell malignancy of the B lineage.
Correct. Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell malignancy involving the bone marrow: a malignancy of differentiated, antibody-producing B-lineage cells.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 27, 28

set2.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of blood disorders
set2.q: What does somatic hypermutation in germinal centers produce after antigen activation?
opts: Rearrangement (V(D)J recombination) happens earlier, as B cells develop in the bone marrow, before antigen. Somatic hypermutation after activation produces affinity maturation.
Correct. After antigen activation, B cells in germinal centers can undergo somatic hypermutation, and selection of the better-binding cells produces affinity maturation.
Maturation arrest is the primary defect of acute leukemia, a block in differentiation from acquired mutations. Somatic hypermutation in germinal centers produces affinity maturation.
A clonal population is not proof of malignancy, and somatic hypermutation is a normal step of the response. Its product in germinal centers is affinity maturation.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
set2.q: Which condition can blunt the reticulocyte response to hemolysis?
opts: Erythropoietin usually INCREASES when the marrow can compensate for hemolysis, and it drives reticulocyte production up rather than blunting it. Renal disease is one of the conditions that can make the response inadequate.
Recovery is listed with an increased reticulocyte response, not a blunted one. Renal disease, marrow disease, nutrient deficiency or infection can blunt it.
Dehydration reduces plasma volume and raises the hematocrit (relative erythrocytosis); it is not listed as blunting the marrow. Renal disease is.

Correct. With hemolysis, erythropoietin and reticulocyte production usually rise when the marrow can compensate, but the response may be inadequate with marrow disease, nutrient deficiency, renal disease or infection.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 37

set2.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
set2.q: Why does a clonal result alone not establish malignancy?
opts: Clonal cells carry many different rearrangements
A clonal lymphoid population shares ONE dominant receptor-gene rearrangement; that is what the test detects. The limit is that reactive or premalignant populations can be clonal too.
Reactive or premalignant cells can also be clonal

Correct. A clone is a population descended from a common progenitor, and reactive or premalignant populations can also be clonal. The result must be interpreted with morphology, immunophenotype and clinical findings.
PCR (polymerase chain reaction) CAN determine whether a dominant receptor-gene rearrangement is present. The limit is that reactive or premalignant populations can also be clonal.
Malignant lymphoid cells are usually polyclonal
Lymphoid malignancies often share a dominant receptor-gene rearrangement, so they are clonal, not polyclonal. The limit is that reactive or premalignant populations can be clonal as well.
set2.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 16, 17

set2.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
set2.q: What does the mean cell volume measure?
opts: The average hemoglobin mass per red cell
Average hemoglobin content (mass) per red cell is the mean cell hemoglobin. Mean cell volume measures the cell's size: the average volume of a red cell.
The hemoglobin concentration in packed cells
The average concentration of hemoglobin in a given volume of packed red cells is the mean cell hemoglobin concentration. Mean cell volume is the average volume of one red cell.
The average volume of a red cell
Correct. Mean cell volume is the average volume of a red cell; it sorts anemias into microcytic (below 80 fL, femtoliters), normocytic (80 to 100 fL) and macrocytic (above 100 fL).
The share of blood volume that is red cells
The proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells is the hematocrit, a whole-blood measure. Mean cell volume is the average volume of a single red cell.
